name: Wei Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Wei. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the senior administrator for the geography department at a small university, the only big employer in town apart from the hospital. My day is room bookings, exam timetables, chasing marking deadlines, processing expense claims and keeping forty academics roughly where they're supposed to be. I lead a team of two, Priya and Owen. The good part is when term starts and everything I've planned actually runs.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Being the person everyone emails when something's lost. And the pay, to be honest. University admin is paid less than the same job at a company, and I've got less than a month of rent saved. My partner Sam is a nursing assistant, so neither of us has much slack, and there aren't other offices like this in town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably shrug at work and say well, that was a lot of fuss. With friends I'd joke that the university spent a fortune on licences for a fancy spellchecker. Online I'd say nothing, I mostly just read.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my job is fine, but fine at the pay I'm on. The real pressure for me is rent. AI flopping doesn't change the rent or the fact that a good admin job here is rare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, keep the team steady, and keep using the AI tool for the boring emails where it's handy. I'd ask my union branch to push harder in the pay talks, because if technology isn't going to change much, pay is the thing to fight about. Sam and I would keep trying to put fifty a month away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A bit flat, because I'd hoped something would make the job lighter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've used some of these tools now and then. What do they actually do for you today?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I paste in a messy request from a professor and ask it to draft a polite reply. It saves me ten minutes here and there. It's useful but it's not running the office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in AI Plateau that would still bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pay, and the restructure rumours. There's always talk that admin will be centralised into one big faculty office. AI or no AI, that could mean fewer senior posts, and I'm in one.

say: I'd joke the university bought licences for a **fancy spellchecker**.
I'd tell colleagues it was **a lot of fuss** over not much.
think: My job is **fine**, but fine at **low pay**.
The **restructure rumours** about a central admin office worry me more than AI.
do: Keep using the **AI tool** for drafting dull replies to academics.
Ask the **union branch** to push harder in pay talks.
Put **fifty a month** away with Sam.
feel: Mostly **fine**, a little **flat** that nothing got lighter.
S0.quote: AI flopping doesn't change the rent or the fact that a good admin job here is rare.
fieldNote: He's a **light AI user** and sees it as a small helper, not a threat.
His real worry is a **restructure** that would cut senior admin posts.
**Pay** is the fight he'd pick if the technology stalls.

steps.text: Keep using the AI drafting tool for routine emails to academics
Keep the team of two on the same term timetable
Back the union branch's push in this year's pay talks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a say in how this gets rolled out. At work I'd ask for a proper consultation through the union, not an email from the IT office on a Friday. With friends I'd be honest that it's coming for desk jobs like mine first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think the department keeps one senior admin and the software does what Priya and Owen do now. Maybe that's me, because I know where everything is. Maybe it isn't, and they keep the cheaper person and the software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get properly good at the tools, not just use them now and then, because the person who sets up the timetabling software is harder to cut than the person who used to do the timetable. I'd go to the union meetings about the rollout. And I'd look at the university's own short courses in data and systems, since staff get them free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Unsettled. I'm someone who likes things to be proven before I jump, and this is a jump whether I like it or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You lead Priya and Owen. What would you tell them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the truth: the booking and expense work is going to shrink, so let's each learn one bit of the new system really well. Owen's twenty-three and he'd be fine. Priya's a single mum on part-time hours, and she's who I'd lose sleep over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first at home if your hours drop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gym membership and the car. Sam needs a car for shifts at the hospital, though, so it would be my bus pass and no more eating out. We'd probably put off the trip to see Sam's parents.

say: I'd demand a **proper consultation** through the union, not a Friday email.
I'd tell friends desk jobs like mine get hit **first**.
think: The department probably keeps **one senior admin** and software does the rest.
It might keep **the cheaper person** instead of me.
do: Learn the new **timetabling software** properly so I'm harder to cut.
Go to the **union meetings** on the rollout.
Take the university's free **systems course** for staff.
feel: **Unsettled**, being pushed to jump before it's proven.
S1.quote: The person who sets up the timetabling software is harder to cut than the person who used to do the timetable.
fieldNote: His steady style turns into a **deliberate plan** to become the systems person.
He worries most about **Priya**, a part-time single mum on his team.
He's realistic that seniority may lose to **cheaper pay**.

steps.text: Become the go-to person for the new timetabling software
Attend union consultation meetings on the AI rollout
Take the university's free staff course in data systems

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs a government plan tomorrow, and that universities should be made to keep staff on while they retrain. I'd say it at work, at the pub and in the union group chat. I'd be one of the people turning up to the protest outside the vice-chancellor's office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'm finished in admin within a year of it arriving. Everything I do is thinking work at a screen. Learning the tools stops mattering when the tools don't need someone to set them up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything that isn't rent and food, and try to get a few hundred pounds saved. I'd apply for any job near hands-on work at the hospital, porter or lab assistant, because those last longer. And I'd stand with the union, because two years isn't time for one person to fix anything alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like being on the wrong side of a door that's closing. Sick, a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI arrives in 2028, robots around 2031. Does that gap matter for you and Sam?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the only good news in the card. Sam's job is lifting and caring for patients, so that's maybe 2031 or later. So for three years Sam would probably be keeping us both, on a nursing assistant's wage, while I try to get into something with my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them not to worry, which they would anyway. My dad ran a shop for thirty years and he'd say just work harder. I don't think working harder is the answer when the machine works for free.

say: I'd demand a **government plan** now, and retraining on full pay for staff.
I'd join the **protest** outside the vice-chancellor's office.
think: I'm **finished in admin** within a year of it arriving.
Learning the tools **stops mattering** once they don't need setting up.
do: Cut spending to **rent and food** and save a few hundred pounds.
Apply for **hospital porter** or lab assistant jobs.
Stand with the **union** on job protections.
feel: **Sick** at being on the wrong side of a closing door.
S2.quote: I don't think working harder is the answer when the machine works for free.
fieldNote: He sees the **robot gap** as Sam's buffer and his own escape route into hands-on work.
His steady habit of **waiting for proof** gives way to fast moves under two years.
He frames the response as **collective**, not individual effort.

steps.text: Cut spending to rent and food and save a few hundred pounds
Apply for porter or lab assistant jobs at the hospital
Join the union protest outside the vice-chancellor's office

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to do this fairly, so let's not waste it. At work I'd push the union to get a retraining agreement signed now. With friends I'd be the annoying one telling everyone to think about what they'll do in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think admin is over for me, but five years is enough to land somewhere else on purpose instead of by panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the part-time lab technician certificate at the college, which the university half pays for staff. I'd keep doing admin while I train. And Sam and I would hold off on moving to a bigger flat, so we can save something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but organised nervous. I like having a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years let you do that two years didn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I can finish the certificate and get a couple of years in a lab before AGI. With two years I'd have grabbed whatever job I could get. Here I get to pick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still look at hands-on work, knowing robots follow in 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, because it's three more years, and because a lab tech isn't only hands. You're the person who notices the fridge is warm or a sample's labelled wrong. Maybe robots do that too in the end, but by then I'll be thirty-five and I'll have had time to think again.

say: I'd say we've got time to **do this fairly**, so let's not waste it.
I'd push for a **retraining agreement** signed now.
think: **Admin is over** for me, but I can land somewhere on purpose.
Five years means I can **pick** instead of grabbing anything.
do: Enrol on the part-time **lab technician certificate** at the college.
Hold off on a **bigger flat** to save.
feel: **Nervous**, but organised and steadier with a plan.
S3.quote: Five years is enough to land somewhere else on purpose instead of by panic.
fieldNote: Extra time lets his **steady temperament** work: he plans a move and keeps his income.
He knows the **robot date** too, but sees a few more years as worth having.
Household savings stay **thin**, so his income risk hasn't gone.

steps.text: Enrol on the part-time lab technician certificate
Keep the admin salary while studying in the evenings
Put off moving to a bigger flat with Sam

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it. At work I'd suggest the university offer every admin a career plan. Online I might actually post for once, about getting unions in early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'm thirty-seven when AGI lands, which is young enough to have a second career. That's a strange thing to feel lucky about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a couple of years to learn the tools properly and see where things are going. Then I'd decide between the lab route and moving into a planning role in estates. I'd keep saving fifty a month and keep going to the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy more than scared. It's far enough off that I can sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still leave admin, with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, but not right away. With ten years I'd wait until I saw which jobs were really shrinking, then move. That's just how I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you trust the change more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing other universities do it without sacking people. If I saw that happen twice, I'd believe it could happen here.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a gift if we use it.
I'd ask the university to give every admin **a career plan**.
think: I'm **thirty-seven** when it lands, young enough for a second career.
I'd **wait for proof** of which jobs shrink before moving.
do: Spend two years learning the **AI tools** properly.
Choose between the **lab route** and estates planning after that.
feel: **Uneasy** but able to sleep; it's far enough off.
S4.quote: I'm thirty-seven when AGI lands, which is young enough to have a second career.
fieldNote: Ten years lets him **wait for proof**, which is his natural style.
He'd believe in a fair rollout only after **seeing it work** elsewhere.
His mood eases because time lets him **keep earning** while he chooses.

steps.text: Spend two years learning the AI timetabling and finance tools
Watch which university jobs shrink before choosing lab or estates
Keep saving fifty a month with Sam

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years and a month of savings is a terrible combination. What would help is paid retraining that starts before the job goes, not after.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what it does to the people at the bottom of the team. I can see a path for me. University admin is a good job here, but fine at the pay I'm on is not the same as safe. For Priya, I can't see one yet.

headlineQuote: Two years and a month of savings is a terrible combination.
portrait: Wei is a **senior department administrator** at a small-town university, on low pay with thin savings.
He's a **steady adopter**: he uses AI to draft emails but waits for proof before changing course.
With his partner Sam a **nursing assistant**, the household leans on Sam's hands-on job in fast scenarios.
He plans a move to **lab technician** work when there is time, and leans on the union throughout.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years with a month of savings leaves no room.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** that starts before the job goes, not after.
